title: Ice Rescue Lake Champlain
description: Petty Officer 3rd Class Lucas Weston and Petty Officer 1st Class Jason Balmer explain how they train for ice rescue search and rescue cases on Lake Champlain, and what safety precautions individuals should take if they are going out on the ice for recreation.
keywords: Ice Rescue, cold weather, Dry Suits, below zero, Coast Guard Station Burlington, 42215204, DVIDS Videos of the Day 012417, training, USCG

transcript.text: (waves lapping)
(intense guitar music)
- We can get a call in the middle of the night,
we need to pull somebody out of the water,
we need to know exactly what we're doing
and how to do it.
- It's important to be at the top of your game,
make sure you're always ready all the time.
- [PO Weston] Yesterday we were out and it was six below
with a wind chill, so as soon as you got out
of the water, everything was freezing.
It's pretty typical for what we're doing.
We'll be out there training two to three hours
and everything will freeze up, the equipment and stuff.
But that's good for us, we learn how to deal with that,
because if we're out there for several hours
looking for somebody, trying to pull someone out
of the water, we'll have to deal with frozen equipment.
- [PO Balmer] We're responsible for the entire lake,
130 miles north to south.
We have a lot of other government agencies that help us
out a lot, fire departments, police departments, they all
have training, they all have equipment.
A lot of times what happens is people go in and they'll
panic, and then they'll just, instead of trying
to get themselves out, they just want to hold onto the ice,
so they get kind of nervous.
So the first thing we'll try to do
is actually try to talk them out of the ice
and kind of give them a demonstration.
Several techniques that we do, we have the cold water
rescue sling which is a yellow sling, it floats.
We have the MARSARS shuttle board.
We can use the rescue sling by itself, we can use
the rescue sling and the shuttle board together.
Couple different techniques we can use
with the shuttle board, we can just slide it out,
have somebody hold onto it, pull them back in,
we can go into the water and get the victim.
It's the last thing we want to do, even with all
the equipment we have.
We want to try to stay as dry as we can.
We also have a 15 foot skiff ice, which is a
inflatable boat.
When we use that we can either push it out,
or we can have a little motor that goes on the back of it.
If we have open water we can use it as a traditional boat.
- [PO Weston] Wear a life jacket, carry some sort of item
that can help get you out of the ice, be it ice saws
or ice pick, and make a float plan with people.
Tell people where you're going, leave them a number
where they can reach you at, let them know how long
you're going to be out, when you anticipate being back,
where exactly you're going.
And if you change anything, let that person know.
(quick guitar music)
